query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that integrates actively‐learned machine‐learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with an analytical framework (e.g., CPA) to explicitly incorporate the impact of extended defects and oxygen impurities will yield significantly more accurate electrical conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr. In particular, when applied over the cryogenic (0–200 K) and elevated (300–1200 K) regimes, the hybrid model will capture defect‐induced electron scattering and finite-temperature relaxations, thereby reducing the error from an order‐of‐magnitude discrepancy (as seen with ideal solution models) to within approximately 30–50% of experimental values.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy with its inherent microstructural defects and extended defect sites, as well as a variant intentionally doped with ~1 wt% oxygen.
generation.intervention: Implement an integrated simulation protocol where actively‐learned MLIPs (such as moment tensor potentials trained on ab initio data across defected configurations) are used to model local atomic relaxations and defect scattering. These outputs are then connected with a CPA-based analytical method to account for long-range disorder and temperature effects.
generation.conditions: Simulations and experiments performed in two regimes: 0–200 K (cryo) and 300–1200 K (elevated). Two sample variants are considered – one near defect-free (low oxygen <0.2 wt%) and one with trace oxygen (~1 wt%).
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic relaxations and modified electron scattering rates at extended defects and oxygen impurity sites that alter the plasma frequency and relaxation time parameters governing electron transport.
generation.mechanism: Defects (including oxygen-induced lattice distortions) alter local electronic states and increase electron scattering compared to a perfect crystal. By capturing these local relaxations and defect configurations through actively learned MLIPs, the approach allows the coupled analytical model to adjust key parameters (like plasma frequency and relaxation time) to more realistically simulate electron conduction across a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The hybrid model is predicted to yield electrical conductivity values that are within approximately 30–50% of experimental measurements in both cryogenic and high-temperature regimes, outperforming conventional analytical predictions based on ideal solutions that can err by up to an order of magnitude.
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical models using the ideal solution 'cocktail' effect and fixed plasma frequency/relaxation time parameters, which assume a perfect, defect-free crystal structure.
generation.boundary: The improved accuracy is expected for BCC HfNbTaTiZr with typical defect densities and oxygen levels around 1 wt%. Predictions may become less reliable if defect concentrations or impurity levels are significantly higher, or for temperature ranges outside 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the successes of spectral conductivity models that account for plasma frequency and relaxation time (evidence from PMC11136967::web::011) and on the demonstrated ability of actively learned MTPs to capture defect effects in multi-principal element alloys (evidence from PMC11275555::web::005). The novel extension here is the coupling of these approaches specifically for electrical conductivity predictions in HfNbTaTiZr with trace oxygen, an aspect not previously covered.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples: one processed to be as defect-free as possible and another intentionally doped with ~1 wt% oxygen. Using techniques such as spark plasma sintering to control processing, perform detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM, SEM) to quantify defect and oxygen distributions. Conduct low-frequency electrical conductivity measurements over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes. Use parallel terahertz spectroscopy to extract plasma frequency and relaxation time. Compare experimental conductivity values to predictions from both the hybrid ML-enhanced/CPA model and existing ideal solution analytical models.
measurements: Electrical conductivity versus temperature (0–200 K and 300–1200 K)
Defect density and oxygen content characterization (via TEM/SEM/EDS)
Plasma frequency and relaxation time (via terahertz spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid model’s predicted conductivity does not improve the accuracy (i.e., if the predicted values differ by more than 50% from experimental measurements) or fail to distinguish between the defect-free and oxygen-doped samples relative to conventional ideal solution predictions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
